title: Narottama Dasa Thakura
html:
Thakura Mahashaya

Narottama Dasa Thakura is a companion of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, although he came into this world only after the Lord had withdrawn from sight. He is called Narottama Dasa, Srila Narottama Dasa Thakura, Paramahamsa Sri Narottama Dasa Thakura; but in Bengal he was known above all as Thakura Mahashaya, or simply Sri Thakura, so that his name hardly needed to be spoken. The title was given to him in Vrindavana by his teacher Sri Jiva Gosvami, in the same days in which he named Srinivasa “Acharya” and Dukhi Krishnadasa “Shyamananda.”1 The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that Jiva, delighted at how quickly his pupil mastered many shastras, “taking everyone's consent,” named him “Sri Mahashaya” (4.422–424).

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” quotes an old verse about him:

“A brahmachari from boyhood, who has seen all the tirthas, the best of the highest bhagavatas — Srila Narottama Dasa.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.279)

So he remained: all his life he kept celibacy, visited the holy places of Vraja, Gauda and Orissa, and became for the Vaishnavas a pattern of pure devotion.

Together with Srinivasa Acharya and Shyamananda he is one of the three great preachers who, in the generation after the Lord, carried the prema-dharma through nama-sankirtana, along the path shown by Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu Himself. When the Lord's associates in Vrindavana withdrew one after another, these three preserved their heritage and widened the movement in Bengal; they are called the threefold power of the Lord's mercy, and of them it is said that they are eternal associates of Gaurasundara who came into the world to carry His message.

Called Before His Birth

Mahaprabhu called Narottama long before he was born. At Ramakeli, in kirtana, the Lord turned His face towards Kheturi — Narottama's future birthplace — and began to call him; His companions did not then understand whom He was calling. That is why the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that Narottama “was born drawn by Krishna Chaitanya” (1.280).

The “Prema-vilasa” tells of this at greater length. On the way back from Kanai-Natshala the Lord, in ecstatic kirtana, began to call out, “Narottama!” Nityananda asked whom He meant, and Mahaprabhu answered: “Your own glory is hidden from you. In Puri you shed tears of love day after day — this prema I gathered and kept. Now I shall leave it in the keeping of the Padmavati, for Narottama.” Then the Lord came to Kutubpur on the bank of the Padmavati, bathed, sang and danced in ecstasy, and told the river to keep His prema and give it to Narottama when he came to bathe; he would be easy to recognise — as soon as he entered the water, the river would overflow its banks. The place was later named Prematali, “the place of prema.”2

The Prince of Kheturi

Narottama took birth at Kheturi in North Bengal, twelve miles from Rampur-Boalia, in the subdivision of Gopalpur in the district of Rajshahi (now in Bangladesh). His father, Raja Krishnananda Datta, held the zamindari of the Gopalpur region on the bank of the Padmavati and a very wealthy man, so that his son was spoken of as a prince. His mother was named Narayani Devi. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says of her: “His mother, most virtuous, was named Narayani; her life was in her son” (1.289). His father's brother, Purushottama Datta, shared with him a wealth and fame that had no equal. Purushottama's son Santosha, Narottama's cousin, later became the raja of Kheturi and his disciple; the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says of him: “He is Sriman Narottama's brother and disciple, pure in serving the guru, Krishna and the Vaishnavas” (1.471).3 Narahari Sarakara Thakura of Srikhanda was very fond of Krishnananda.

The family belonged to the kayastha community. One of the biographies explains that Krishna let His associate be born in such a family to make it plain that His associates may appear in any station of life. Later the smartas would call Narottama a “shudra”; how his own life answered them, and how Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati judges the matter, will be told below.

His appearance was on the full moon of the month of Magha — according to one of the biographies, around the middle of the fifteenth century of the Shaka era:

“Narottama was born on the full-moon day of the month of Magha; day by day he grew like the moon.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.281)

The “Narottama-vilasa” also names the Magha purnima and specifies the hour — the sixth danda. According to our calendar (Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math), the Appearance Day of Srila Narottama Dasa Thakura is the purnima at the end of the month of Madhava (≈ Magha); in 2026 it fell on 1 February.4

At his birth there were auspicious signs. In his joy the raja gave generous gifts to the brahmanas, and they foretold that the boy was a great soul through whom many would be delivered; the “Prema-vilasa” also tells of Narayani's prophetic dream and of the astrologer's prediction. Day by day the child grew as the moon grows: his body had the lustre of melted gold, his eyes the shape of lotus petals, his arms reached his knees, his navel was deep — all marks of a mahapurusha — and the townspeople gathered to look at the beautiful holy child. The rite of first feeding, the anna-prashana, was performed with lavish gifts; the “Narottama-vilasa” adds that from then on the boy ate only the prasada of Vishnu. His mother, floating in bliss, would not let him out of her sight and cared for him unceasingly; in the women's quarters he was petted with great joy, and he himself was so quiet that wherever he was laid, there he lay.

When the time came for study, his intelligence amazed everyone: he remembered a thing after hearing it once, and before long Sanskrit grammar, rhetoric, poetry and many shastras were his. But soon he came to regard as useless any knowledge that does not lead to Hari-bhajana, and he thought of the sages of old who went to the forest to serve Hari. From early childhood he was drawn to bhakti and indifferent to games and pleasures. Hearing from devotees of the glory of Nityananda and Gauranga, he seemed to come alive anew: day and night he repeated Their names and meditated on Their qualities, and in dreams the Lord would often come to him with His associates. The “Narottama-vilasa” says that a brahmana named Krishnadasa told him about the Lord, and that in a dream Gaura, Nityananda, Advaita and Their associates told him to go to Vrindavana, to Lokanatha.

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says:

“To Sri Krishna Chaitanya, Nityananda, Advaita and Their associates he offers his prayers, and tears stream from both his eyes. In the guise of a dream the Lord with His associates appeared to him, comforted His beloved Narottama and calmed him.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.285–286)

Prema from the Hands of the Padmavati

When Narottama was twelve years old, Nityananda, in a dream, bade him bathe in the Padmavati and receive the prema kept for him. The next morning, as soon as he stepped into the water, the river overflowed its banks, and the Padmavati, remembering the Lord's words, gave him what had been entrusted to her. This wonder is not the power of a river: the Padmavati only returned what the Lord had given into her keeping — the mercy of Mahaprabhu and Nityananda, Nityananda's tears of love. Having bathed at Prematali, Narottama was at once filled with prema and resolved to leave his family and go to Vrindavana.

Leaving Home

From that time he was completely changed — in temper, in looks, in everything. His parents tried by every means to bring him back to what he had been, but in vain: one intoxicated with divine love could no longer be held by family ties. Fearing that their son would suddenly leave for Vrindavana, the raja and Narayani set guards over him, while he begged Gaura and Nityananda to show him the way and sang: “Hari, Hari, when shall I become a resident of Vrindavana?”

The opportunity came of itself. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” relates:

“Suddenly a man came from the king of Gauda, and his father and uncle went to the court in Gauda. Taking this opportunity he deceived the guards and somehow took leave of his mother. [...] The mother lives carefree, cherishing her son, and does not know that her son will leave home. Narottama, meanwhile, in deep secrecy set out, meditating on the feet of the Lord. How fresh his youth, how handsome he is! On the full-moon day of Kartika he left home.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.287–288, 1.290–292)

He deceived the guards not out of guile: this is how one leaves whom the Lord has called. Young and handsome, he went away without a thought for youth, or beauty, or a kingdom.5

The son of a wealthy zamindar, for the sake of meeting the Lord he gave up every bodily comfort in an instant. He walked day and night barefoot and in tears, with no thought of food or drink, until at last he collapsed senseless beneath a tree. A brahmana with a golden complexion then approached, offered him a bowl of milk and spoke gently: “Narottama, drink — your wounds will heal; be calm, all will be well,” and vanished. And that night in a dream Rupa and Sanatana placed their hands upon his breast and fed him milk brought by Mahaprabhu Himself, and his weariness left him. Pilgrims, seeing that he was a raja's son, grew fond of him. He lived now on milk, now on roots and fruits: his longing to see Vrindavana drowned his hunger. On the way he heard from devotees about Gaura and Nityananda and prayed to Nityananda, “When, Nitai-chand…” At Mathura, on the bank of the Yamuna, remembering the six Gosvamis headed by Rupa and Sanatana, he wept in ecstasy.

Keeping the Lord's feet in his heart, he visited many tirthas and came to Vrindavana (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.293).

Lokanatha's Only Disciple

Of the six Gosvamis, three still remained in Vrindavana at that time — Gopala Bhatta, Jiva and Raghunatha Dasa; Rupa, Sanatana and others had already withdrawn from sight.6 The senior Gosvamis of Vraja took the young man to their hearts: “Sri Gopala Bhatta and all the other wise ones regard Narottama as their second life” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.347).

Jiva Gosvami sent him to serve the feet of Lokanatha Gosvami; according to the “Prema-vilasa,” Sri Rupa told Jiva to do so in a dream. Lokanatha accepted no disciples — such was his vow. But Narottama was drawn by his severe renunciation and vowed to take initiation from him alone. So he began to serve him in secret, at night: he cleaned the place where Lokanatha went to relieve himself, brought sifted earth and water for cleansing, and hid the broom. This went on for a long time — according to one of the biographies, a whole year — until Lokanatha, catching the raja's son at this work one night, softened his resolve. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says it briefly:

“At that very time Narottama came there and joyfully served his guru as is fitting. Pleased with his service, he gave him the mantra of initiation and showed Narottama boundless mercy.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.345–346)

And of the day of initiation:

“On the full moon of the month of Shravana, at an auspicious moment, Lokanatha accepted Narottama as his disciple.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.294)

According to the “Prema-vilasa,” he received initiation in the month of Vaishakha.7 Thus Narottama became Lokanatha's only disciple; the story is told in detail in the article on Lokanatha Gosvami.

Narottama's initiation is a lesson for the whole world: how to serve one's spiritual master, and how selfless, sincere service can move to mercy even one bound by a vow never to accept a disciple. This is not “menial work” but a disciple's model service; Lokanatha and Narottama enacted this pastime to show its worth, above all for the people of North Bengal. Centuries later it was repeated by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati and Srila Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji: the Babaji too had vowed to accept no disciples, and Bhaktisiddhanta by persistent service won his acceptance — as his only disciple.

At Jiva's Feet

In Vrindavana Narottama lived by madhukari, on alms, and studied the writings of the Gosvamis under the guidance of Sri Jiva. Here, with Jiva, he met Srinivasa. Srinivasa had only heard his name before — and the name alone filled him with joy and longing to meet him; in a dream Sri Rupa told him, “Tomorrow you will see him.” The next day they met, and tears flowed from the eyes of both. “Providence has been kind,” said Srinivasa, “it has brought me such a jewel as Narottama,” and Narottama bowed to him and humbly begged his mercy. From their first meeting they were friends for life and studied together; to Jiva the two were “like his two arms” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.405–426). Jiva himself decided to show the two the holy forests, and when Raghava Gosvami came from Govardhana he told him: “Srinivasa and Narottama will go with you” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 5.11). Raghava led them through the whole of Vraja-mandala and showed them the places of Krishna's pastimes, and he loved them both exceedingly, “regarding the two as one” (5.29). Narahari Chakravarti gives this circuit the whole fifth wave of the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” the longest in the book; at its close Raghava tells them: “Birth after birth you two are servants of the Lord” (5.3776). The “Anuraga-valli” (6) also tells of their farewell circuit of Vraja.8

Then Dukhi Krishnadasa, the future Shyamananda, came from Gauda. That very day Srinivasa noticed auspicious signs and said he would surely meet some Vaishnava, and Narottama replied: “The one I have heard about — that very Duhkhi Krishnadasa will meet us here” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 6.10) — and he came. From then on the three studied with Jiva together, and he taught each of them closely, opening to them the philosophy and scriptures of Mahaprabhu and a devotion full of bliss, and the three studied deeply the works of the six Gosvamis. All three were accomplished musicians, skilled in kalavati, the music of Delhi, and with Jiva's permission they held kirtanas. One heart, one life and one aim united them in their bhajana in Vrindavana, and yet they felt that their innermost longing was still unfulfilled.

Narahari describes their life in Vraja as a life within the pastimes themselves. At times Srinivasa and Narottama stayed at Govardhana. Once, entering a cave, they heard the sound of the flute and caught the fragrance of Krishna's body — and both fell unconscious; coming to, they saw a cowherd boy who said he was guarding them, and vanished. At night Krishna came to them in a dream: “In the guise of a cowherd boy I gave you darshan” (6.199). At Radha-kunda Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami showered his mercy on them, and on the path by which Radhika goes to the temple of the Sun they heard the jingling of Her anklets (6.178–211). Of Narottama's service within the mind the “Bhakti-ratnakara” tells:

“Narottama, in the form of a maidservant, with great care boils down milk at the sakhi's sign. Seeing the milk boil over, he was alarmed and took the milk pot off the stove with his hands. His hand was burnt — he had no awareness of it at all; having boiled down the milk, he gave it to the sakhi. With joy in [their] hearts [they] fed Radha and Krishna; as soon as [he] received the remnants, he came back to outer awareness. As soon as he saw his burnt hand, he concealed it; some intimate person knew the secret.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 6.171–175)

His mind, Narahari adds, “always wanders in Navadvipa and Vrindavana” (6.177).

Krishnadasa Kaviraja wrote the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” while Jiva was still living, and soon afterwards the three future acharyas came to Vrindavana. That, says one of the biographies, is why the “Charitamrita” names neither Srinivasa nor Narottama, Lokanatha's disciple: the book was finished before they began to preach (and Lokanatha, moreover, had forbidden any mention of himself). Narottama regarded Krishnadasa Kaviraja himself as the centre of the circle of devotees after the six Gosvamis and drew inspiration from him.

The Gosvamis' Books to Gauda

Jiva grieved over the wretched state of Gauda and wished to establish his disciples there as acharyas; the Gosvamis of Vraja decided the same. The “Prema-vilasa” (12) says the decision was taken at Jiva's festival at the end of the month of Kartika. For their deep learning and devotion the three were charged with preaching bhakti according to the Gosvamis' teaching, and Jiva told them: “From now on carry Mahaprabhu's message everywhere. Take the books of the Gosvamis and go quickly to Bengal.” Lokanatha too told Narottama to return to his homeland and preach.

Before setting out the three took leave of all the Gosvamis. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami embraced Narottama and Shyamananda; Gopala Bhatta said to Narottama: “May Sri Radha-ramana fulfill your desires!” (6.415). Lokanatha, embracing them all and bathing them in tears, said to Jiva: “The charge of all of them rests entirely on you” (6.427). On the last night in Vrindavana Narottama lamented the parting so that, in Narahari's words, “on hearing it, wood and stone melt” (6.483).

The books were packed in a wooden chest protected from the rain and loaded on an ox-cart; a wealthy man of Mathura paid for the cart and for guards on foot, and Jiva accompanied them to Mathura and beyond, and at parting entrusted Narottama and Shyamananda to Srinivasa (6.525–533). They set out on the fifth day of the bright half of the month of Agrahayana (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 6.231) — according to one of the biographies, in the year 1504 of the Shaka era (1582–1583). Bowing to Govinda, Gopinatha and Madana-mohana, the three followed the cart along the road to Mathura, spending the nights in villages and holding sankirtana and preaching there. Among those who saw them off was Uddhava Dasa (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 6.514). The “Prema-vilasa” (12–13) also tells of this journey.

In Vana-Vishnupura the books were stolen at night by the men of King Vira Hambira, who took the chest for treasure. The next morning the grief of the three was so great that life lost all meaning for them: “Narottama says, ‘I shall give up my life’” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 7.111). Learning that the books were to be sought from the king in Vishnupura, Srinivasa stayed there, and, knowing Lokanatha's intention, said to Narottama: “Go quickly to the village of Kheturi and carry out the order of Prabhu Lokanatha” (7.119), and told him to send Shyamananda on from there to Utkala.9 So Narottama returned to his homeland. “Who can understand this lila of the Mahashaya?” says the “Bhakti-ratnakara.” “On arriving, the very first thing he did was to infuse spiritual power (shakti) into Sri Santosha” (7.124). Soon a messenger of Vira Hambira came to Kheturi with a letter from Srinivasa: the books had been found. Narottama told the news to his cousin Santosha and wrote to Srinivasa, and separately to Vira Hambira; the queen of Vishnupura, hearing that letter, prayed to see “Thakura Mahashaya Narottama” even once (7.240–277). Narottama sent Shyamananda off to Utkala, promising to meet him in Nilachala (7.294–310); according to one of the biographies, Shyamananda stayed with him in Kheturi for some months. How Srinivasa recovered the books and how Vira Hambira was converted is told in the article on Srinivasa Acharya.

Why did Lokanatha let his only disciple go? Narottama's former position as a wealthy zamindar made him especially fit to preach in North Bengal: he above all could teach the people of that land the norms of a renounced life. Lokanatha saw in him not only a noble upbringing but also zeal and a liking for being among people, and out of compassion for them he told him to return to Kheturi. Hermits absorbed in intimate service are usually not inclined to work for the “good” of people: such good, while it remains on the bodily level, is valued only by those who have not understood the true aim of life. But when a devotee of Narottama's stature takes up such work, the work itself is ennobled. So, through his disciple, Lokanatha was instructing the world — as a mother-in-law, instructing her daughter, teaches her daughter-in-law.

Narottama himself, tormented by separation from his guru, obeyed and set about preaching pure devotional service in North Bengal. His humility and sorrow sound in the song of the “Prarthana” “Aneka duhkhera pare…”: after many sorrows he was brought to Vraja — and now he is far from it once more.

In the Lord's Footsteps

On receiving word from Shyamananda in Utkala, Narottama set out for the darshan of Navadvipa and other holy places (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 7.468). First of all he came to Mahaprabhu's birthplace, Mayapur-Navadvipa. As he approached, he grieved that he had not been born in the days when Gauranga's sankirtana never ceased there: “Such a wealth of joy I did not get to see!” (8.13). Nadia appeared to him now in the bliss of kirtana, now in sorrow, and in tears he sat down under an ashvattha tree. An old brahmana came there every day: under that tree Nimai had once studied the shastras with His students, and one day the brahmana had seen Him there again. Learning who Narottama was, the old man burst into tears and told him of the former happiness of Nadia and of that secret. Narottama took the dust of his feet, and the brahmana blessed him: “Always gain bhakti, my son” (8.69) — and showed him the way to Mayapur, to the house of Shachi and Jagannatha Mishra.

At the door of that house Narottama fell down in tears. Inside he was met by Shuklambara Brahmachari, who at once guessed that this was “the Narottama whom the Lord drew [to Himself] in the village of Ramakeli” (8.83), embraced him and asked him endlessly about the Gosvamis of Vrindavana. Ishana Thakura, Shachi-mata's old servant, embraced Narottama too. In Shuklambara's house he saw Damodara Pandita, a direct associate of the Lord, and fell at his feet in great emotion (8.93); Damodara introduced him to Shripati, Shrinidhi and the rest. And those of the Lord's associates who had already withdrawn — “all of them gave him their darshan in the guise of dreams” (8.99). All these aged associates of the Lord were sunk in grief over His withdrawal.10 Letting Narottama go, Ishana told him to hurry to Puri, and from there to Srikhanda and Katwa: “Together with Srinivasa you will come here again” (8.109).

Narottama spent several days in Mayapur, then came to Shantipura, to Advaita's house. Advaita had already withdrawn from the world's sight, yet the day before He had told Achyutananda of the guest, and to Narottama himself, “unseen by others,” He revealed Himself together with His associates (8.116, 8.121). Achyutananda and Narottama recognised each other without any introduction; Advaita's son asked the guest about the Gosvamis of Vrindavana, together they sang the glory of Mahaprabhu, and Advaita's associates kept him for three or four days.11 Crossing the Ganga, in Ambika-Kalna, in the house of Gauridasa Pandita, he bowed to the Deities of Nitai and Chaitanya and met Gauridasa's disciple Hridaya Chaitanya, and they embraced. In Saptagrama, at the confluence of the Ganga, Yamuna and Sarasvati, a village blessed by Nityananda, he visited Uddharana Datta's home; its master had left this world only a few days before, and the devotees lived in the anguish of separation from their guru.

In Kharadaha Parameshvari Dasa led him into the inner apartments, to Jahnava and Vasudha, with whom Virabhadra was also present. Seeing that he bore the mercy of Lokanatha and Jiva, the two mistresses granted him incomparable mercy; for several days he spoke with them about Krishna, and they said of him: “The name ‘Mahashaya’ befits him” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.215). Parameshvari described the road to Puri to him in detail; Narottama was granted darshana of Mahesha Pandita's feet, and at parting Mahesha and the others could not calm themselves for love (8.220). In Khanakul-Krishnanagara Narottama came to Abhirama Gopala Thakura. He lived in separation from Nityananda, hardly returning to outer consciousness; Narottama wept much, beheld the wonderful Deity of Abhirama's Gopinatha and offered Him prayers, and Abhirama together with his wife Malini showed him much mercy and bade him go quickly to Nilachala (8.225).

In Puri he was awaited: Gopinatha Acharya, Kanai Khutiya, Shikhi Mahiti and others “all had an earlier order from the Lord to console Narottama in Nilachala” (8.231). “I was just hoping you would come today,” said Gopinatha. Narottama fell at the feet of the Lord's associates, and they spoke long of Krishna, Gauranga and the Gosvamis. They took him to Jagannatha, Baladeva and Subhadra, and then Gopinatha gave him the brahmana Jagannatha Dasa as a guide, who led him through the places of the Lord's pastimes. At the samadhi of Haridasa Thakura Narottama wept beyond description, he visited the Gambhira, and at the abode of Gadadhara Pandita cried aloud, “O life of Gauranga, O Gadadhara!” He had darshana of Tota-Gopinatha. Mamu Gosvami, Gadadhara's disciple, who served Gopinatha, took him to a secluded spot in the garden and told him of the pastimes of the Lord and Gadadhara: here Gadadhara read the “Bhagavata” and the Lord listened; here, into the temple of Gopinatha, the Lord entered and did not come out again (8.357); here Gadadhara too withdrew. Hearing of the Lord's withdrawal, Narottama fell unconscious, and everyone wept. Mamu Gosvami sent him off with these words:

“From Nilachala go quickly to the land of Gauda and, giving bhakti, bring the living beings to fulfilment. Lord Chaitanya's mercy is upon you; you will destroy the misfortune of many people. You will be immersed in the ocean of the joy of sankirtana; in great bliss you will reveal the Lord's innermost desires.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.378–380)

Everywhere in Puri he was honoured as the one whom the Lord had called before his birth.

In the house of Kashi Mishra Gopala Guru received him with great love. He showed Narottama the Lord's bed and seat and the places of His ecstasies, and both wept; he told him about Vakreshvara and entrusted him to the feet of Sri Radhakanta (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.382–392). Narottama had darshana of the Deities of the Radhakanta Matha, and the brahmana Jagannatha showed him the chariot road where the Lord had danced, the Gundicha temple, the garden where the Lord and His associates took prasada, and the Indradyumna-sarovara (8.393–403). The “Narottama-vilasa” (4) relates that in Puri he dreamed of the Lord's kirtana before the chariot. At parting the devotees of Puri said: “We shall not see Srinivasa again; you will give him all this news” (8.406).

From Puri he went to Nrisimhapura, to Shyamananda. Shyamananda came out with his followers to meet him — he “seemed to regain his life” (8.414) — and they spent days and nights in conversation; then Shyamananda himself set out for Nilachala. In Srikhanda Narahari Sarakara, hearing of Narottama's arrival, remembered meeting his father: “He is a ruler, Krishnananda Raya by name” (8.423), embraced him and blessed him: “You will live long and will spread bhakti” (8.430); Raghunandana embraced him too. His hosts asked about the devotees of Puri. Raghunandana showed him the Deity of Gaura installed by Narahari, and Narottama in ecstasy bowed down in the courtyard (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.431–432).

From Srikhanda Raghunandana sent him to Yajigrama, to Srinivasa. Srinivasa came out of the house, embraced Narottama before he could bow, listened long to his account of Navadvipa and Nilachala, and then said:

“You must go to the village of Kheturi without delay. What is there to say — soon it will be revealed what this is for: you will arrange the service of the Deity. With everyone I shall soon come there; do not worry if there is some delay in this.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.441–443)

In Katwa, Kantaka-nagara, he was received by Gadadhara Dasa, who lived in separation from Gaura and Nityananda; he embraced Narottama, bathing him in tears, and entrusted him to the feet of Gaurachandra, the Deity he served. Seeing that Deity, Narottama could not contain his feelings, and at the place where the Lord took sannyasa he fell unconscious (8.445–455). The “Narottama-vilasa” (5) relates that in Yajigrama and Srikhanda he learned of the withdrawal of almost all the Lord's associates in Puri. In Ekachakra an old brahmana showed him the places of Nityananda's pastimes; remembering Hadai Pandita and Padmavati, Nityananda's parents, Narottama fell unconscious. That brahmana was Nityananda Himself: “Prabhu could not deceive Narottama” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.462) — Narottama beheld Him as Nityananda-Balarama, and the Lord forbade him to reveal this to others (8.463–464); the “Narottama-vilasa” says the same.

At last, by his guru's will, he returned home. Asking the way, he came to the Padmavati, crossed it and arrived in Kheturi, where the people came out to meet him. They rejoiced — and feared: would one who had renounced the world stay in his former kingdom? And then, says the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” “a voice came from the sky: ‘Here Narottama will dwell joyfully without cease. Having appeared [in the world] by the Lord's will, he delivers the unbelievers, giving them the gift of bhakti’” (8.477–478). His father and uncle had by then left this world. Santosha, the best of the saintly people of the village, ran out onto the road, prostrated himself before him and with tears took the dust of his feet, and Narottama embraced him. The “Prema-vilasa” (13) tells of his return and of his instructions to Shyamananda.

The Six Deities of Kheturi

The estate passed to Santosha Datta, and he became raja. Narottama had long since renounced the world and laid claim to nothing, and Santosha became his disciple: after a few days Narottama initiated him into the mantra of Radha-Krishna. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” calls him just that: “Sri Mahashaya's disciple is Sri Santosha Datta” (10.205). Santosha had long wished to build a temple and install a Deity, and he asked for permission. Within a few months he raised a large temple, and with it a storehouse for provisions, a hall for kirtana, dwellings and an ashrama for devotees, a tank, a garden of flowers and a house for guests.

While still in Vrindavana, Lokanatha had told Narottama to install Deities of Radha-Krishna and Sri Gauranga. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says:

“When Narottama came to Gauda, Prabhu Lokanatha gave the command: the service of the Deities of Sri Gauranga and Krishna, service to the Sri Vaishnavas, and the Lord's sankirtana. As he was commanded, so he applied himself: he established the service of six beautiful Deities. With all earnestness he is always absorbed in their service; the very sound of those names soothes the heart.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.422–425)

On his return Narottama prepared five pairs of Radha-Krishna Deities — the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (10.191) speaks of five Krishnas with Their beloveds; the sixth was Gauranga. By Lokanatha's command Shyamananda too was invited to the festival.

This is how Gauranga appeared. According to one of the biographies, the night before Narottama received an instruction in a dream; the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says only: “I do not know what came into Sri Thakura's mind” (10.196). At daybreak he went to a small village near Gopalpur and asked to be let into the granary of a certain Vipradasa — “a fortunate [man] named Vipradasa,” as the “Bhakti-ratnakara” calls him (10.193) — a granary for rice and mustard seed. They politely tried to dissuade him: venomous snakes had settled there, hissing terribly, and snake-charmers could not drive them out either with mantras or with remedies. “Do not worry; the snakes will run away,” Narottama smiled (10.200). The granary was opened — the snakes, to everyone's amazement, had vanished, and the Deities of Sri Gaura and Vishnupriya came into his hands of Their own accord: “From the granary Sri Gaurasundara with His beloved came into his arms, and [this] was visible to every eye” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.202). A mighty sankirtana broke out on the spot. Narottama brought Them to Kheturi and established Their service; today these Deities are served in Gambhila. According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (10.191–206), this was still before the great festival, during the preparations for it.12 The “Prema-vilasa” (19) says that the form of Gauranga was manifested by the Lord Himself before He took sannyasa.

So six Deities appeared in Kheturi: Sri Gauranga, Sri Vallavikanta, Sri Vrajamohana, Sri Krishna, Sri Radhakanta and Sri Radharamana.13 The very sound of these names gladdens the hearts of the devotees; Narottama composed a pranama to Them:

“Gauranga, Vallavikanta, Sri Krishna, Vrajamohana, Radha-ramana, O Radha, Radha-kanta — obeisance to You!” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.426)

After the arati he would worship Them, calling each Deity by name (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.492, 495–496). Srila Vamshidasa Babaji spoke of Them with a loving jest: “Six thieves in the house of Narottama Thakura, and one thief in Mayapur.”

By revealing Vishnupriya together with Gaura, Narottama gave the world a lesson in siddhanta. Some held Gaurasundara to be not Vishnu but merely a jiva within varnashrama, a “great man” or the founder of a sect; Narottama dispelled this error by revealing, together with Gaura-Narayana, Vishnupriya — the bhu-shakti, one of His three energies. Following him as “his first teacher,” Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura installed Gaura and Vishnupriya in the Lord's house in Mayapur. But this worship is on the pure path of the followers of Rupa, walked by Rupa, Raghunatha, Jiva, Krishnadasa Kaviraja and Narottama himself: Krishna is worshipped together with His ashraya-vigraha. Where this path is abandoned and Gaura with Vishnupriya are “worshipped” as separate from Krishna, in a worldly fashion of one's own, there is neither Vishnupriya nor Gaurasundara. The installation of the six Deities is described in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (10, 12), the “Prema-vilasa” (19) and the “Narottama-vilasa” (6).

The Great Festival at Kheturi

Santosha Datta resolved to mark the installation of the six Deities with a festival such as Gauda had never seen. It was set for the Phalguna Purnima, the appearance day of Mahaprabhu. In its splendour it was compared only with Yudhishthira's rajasuya. Messengers were sent many miles to invite kings and landholders, poets and pandits, Vaishnavas, the best singers and reciters.

Narottama was waiting for Srinivasa. Srinivasa meanwhile had married, had been to Vrindavana once more, and was now staying in Budhari, in the house of his disciple Ramachandra Kaviraja. There came the brahmana Durgadasa of Kheturi — “Sri Thakura Narottama… lifted [me] out of the pit of the filth of worldly things,” he said of himself — and told Srinivasa how Narottama, on coming back from Nilachala, had “refuted the doctrines of the pashandas,” made five Deities of Krishna and obtained Gaura in Vipradasa's granary (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.184–209). The next day Narottama himself came. Srinivasa embraced him and could not let him go, and Narottama said:

“Prabhu ordered me to go to Gauda [for] the service of the Deities, the service of the Vaishnavas, and Sri sankirtana. And in this the Deities showed Their mercy, and the temple and all the other requisites came about. On the full moon of Phalguna the Deities you yourself would seat upon the throne — this was in my mind.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.254–256)

Here Narottama first saw Ramachandra. The night before, Gaurasundara had appeared to Ramachandra in a dream: “You are dear to Me, and Narottama is dear to Me; seeing each other, you two will remember what was before. You two will bestow My prema-bhakti and free living beings from the cruel threefold suffering” (10.232–233). And, beholding Narottama, Ramachandra lost his composure, “remembering what had been before” (10.250). In a dream the Lord told Srinivasa too to send out the invitations quickly: letters went with fifteen messengers to Navadvipa and other places, and separately to Shyamananda in Utkala (10.266–277). Srinivasa entrusted Ramachandra to Narottama and sent them to Kheturi, saying, “I will come soon” (10.286–289). The “Narottama-vilasa” (6) tells of this as well; the “Prema-vilasa” (14) speaks of a first festival, when Gauranga and Vallavikanta were installed.

At Narottama's invitation there came all who still remained of Sri Chaitanya's associates, and their disciples — from Navadvipa, Orissa, Kharadaha and other places. From Kharadaha came Jahnava, Nityananda's shakti, with her retinue; with her were Parameshvari Dasa, her uncle Krishnadasa Sarkhel, Nityananda's son-in-law Madhava Acharya, Raghupati Vaidya, Minaketana Ramadasa, Murari Chaitanya Dasa, Jnana Dasa, Mahidhara, Shankara, Kamalakara Pippalai, Gauranga Dasa, Nakari, Krishnadasa, Damodara, Balarama Dasa, Mukunda and Vrindavana Dasa Thakura. From Srikhanda came Raghunandana and others, from Navadvipa Shripati and Shrinidhi, from Shantipura Advaita's sons Achyutananda, Gopala and Krishna Mishra, from Ambika-Kalna Hridaya Chaitanya, from Nrisimhapura Shyamananda with his people. Srinivasa with the devotees set out from Budhari, from the house of Govinda Kaviraja. Achyutananda was received with great reverence: the festival took place almost half a century after the Lord's withdrawal. Srinivasa, with his disciple Ramachandra and Govinda, Ramachandra's younger brother, laboured to make the festival a success. When Srinivasa arrived in Kheturi, Narottama came out to meet him with Ramachandra, Santosha Datta presented his people to him, and Narottama himself led him to the Deities (10.331–349).

Santosha provided a huge boat for the crossing, palanquins and carts. Srinivasa, Narottama and the raja met the guests with garlands; when Jahnava entered Kheturi with kirtana, Srinivasa, Narottama and Shyamananda, walking ahead of all, prostrated themselves before her in the dust of the road. Each guest was given a separate house and servants. Gates and houses were decorated with banana leaves, pots, mango leaves, flowers and auspicious signs; there rose mountains of clay and silver vessels of milk and ghee, thousands of pots of yogurt, mountains of vegetables and fruits.

On the eve, at Jahnava's word, the preparations were completed. Narottama honoured Jahnava with sandal paste and garlands; at the request of Narottama and Srinivasa, Raghunandana Thakura sang the mangalacharana, the sankirtana went on until midnight, and thousands of people received maha-prasada.

On the day of the festival the rites of installation and the abhisheka of the six Deities were performed by Srinivasa Acharya as chief priest — all the Lord's associates gave him leave for this (10.479) — and the whole installation took place under Jahnava's guidance, according to her instructions. He gave the Deities the names the Lord had made known in a dream (10.482). An hour before the abhisheka the Deities were carried into the temple; then came the dressing and ornaments, thousands of dishes, tambula, sandal paste, garlands, a great arati and dandavats by all. Srinivasa, Narottama and Shyamananda gave everyone sandal paste and garlands, and at Jahnava's word Nrisimha Chaitanya Dasa garlanded the three of them. Jahnava sat on a high seat in the kirtana hall.

Jahnava, looking at Narottama with a merciful glance, “joyfully infused [into him] — I do not know what power” (10.522); Achyutananda too showed him favour, and at their word and with the mahantas' permission Narottama began the kirtana. His companions were the finest masters of song and music: Devidasa played the mardala, Vallava (Vallabha) Dasa and Gauranga Dasa the kansya-tala and other instruments, Gokula sang the alapa (10.527–533). Raghunandana of Srikhanda put garlands and sandal paste on Narottama and his companions. First Narottama sang of Gauranga absorbed in the bhava of Sri Radhika, and then of the pastimes of Radha and Krishna. His sweet kirtana, with its distinctive melody, filled all directions, and everyone wept tears of prema. In the crowd people said:

“Mahaprabhu used to hear from Svarupa lofty songs with great joy in His heart. To preserve the tradition of song and to dispel regret, He thoroughly considered in His heart how to spread [it]. At that time He kept it in a casket of prema; now, through Narottama, the Lord has opened it.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.556–558)

And then in this kirtana Mahaprabhu Himself appeared with His associates. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” compares His appearance to lightning in a cloud (10.572). With Him were Nityananda and Advaita, Gadadhara Pandita, Haridasa and Srivasa, Svarupa Damodara, Narahari, Mukunda, Gauridasa Pandita, Madhava, Vasu and Govinda Ghosha, Acharya Purandara, Mahesha, Shankara, Shridhara, Jagadisha Pandita, Yadunandana, Kashishvara, Rupa and Sanatana and many others; among them danced Achyutananda, Raghunandana, Shripati and Shrinidhi. “With a gentle, gentle smile He looks toward Narottama; Prabhu Nityananda knows that sign of the Lord” (10.580). Those who had long since withdrawn from the world's sight appeared again and sang in the sankirtana as in the Lord's days, and the devotees in their joy forgot that They had ever withdrawn. Embracing Narottama and Srinivasa, the Lord spoke to them tenderly, and then, together with the unmanifest associates, suddenly withdrew again. Everyone was stricken with grief — even the pashandas who had come to mock wept — and the festival was not resumed at once.

This was no vision of the dead and no ghosts: the Lord's eternal associates do not die — they only withdraw from the world's sight and by Their own will appear again. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that on that day Srinivasa, Narottama and their companions saw every desire of theirs fulfilled (10.607). Jahnava consoled everyone: “Full mercy [has been shown] to Narottama and Srinivasa. What the Lord ordered has come true: together with His associates He danced in such a kirtana” (10.628–629). The “Prema-vilasa” (19) adds that Radha and Krishna appeared above the kirtana, and Narottama was plunged into deep ecstasy.

Then Jahnava sprinkled the Deities with red powder — phagu — and the devotees played with it. In the evening Srinivasa performed the abhisheka of Gauranga in honour of His appearance, to Narahari's song of the Lord's appearance on the Phalguna Purnima; the kirtana went on all night, and at dawn the mangala-arati was performed. Early in the morning Jahnava bathed and with great enthusiasm cooked innumerable dishes and herself served prasada to the mahantas (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.686–687).14 She asked Narottama, Srinivasa and Shyamananda to eat after the mahantas, and she herself ate last; outside the hall Santosha fed thousands of people and also ate last.

On the second lunar day, at the request of Srinivasa, who was fulfilling Santosha's wish, the guests cooked for the Deities themselves in their own lodgings, and Santosha tearfully presented everyone with gold coins, cloth, ornaments and vessels (10.712–721). The mahantas dispersed to their own lands, and Jahnava with her retinue left for Vrindavana. Srinivasa stayed on in Kheturi for a while, and every day he and Narottama sang kirtana in the Lord's courtyard — where Gaura, Nityananda and Advaita had danced with Their associates; then he left with Shyamananda for Budhari. Narottama and Ramachandra remained in Kheturi: “Showing favor to many hundreds of pashandas, they make [them] fit for the Lord's prema-bhakti” (10.771). The festival was truly unprecedented, and Vaishnavas still remember it today. The “Narottama-vilasa” (8) tells of the farewell to the mahantas and of robbers who on the road took shelter of the Vaishnavas.

The Lord's courtyard in Kheturi became the heart of kirtana: “Narottama revealed the glory of that courtyard,” and he was always grey with its dust (11.13–14). Once, on a full-moon night, when he was singing of the rasa-lila, all four quarters suddenly grew bright, “like lightning in a cloud,” a fragrance spread and anklets jingled; and when it all vanished, everyone fell unconscious: “This is the supramundane lila of Krishna with His Beloved” (11.22–26).

Returning from Vrindavana, Jahnava came first of all to Kheturi, and she was met by the devotees headed by Narottama and Ramachandra Kaviraja (“Narottama-vilasa” 9; “Prema-vilasa” 15; “Bhakti-ratnakara” 11.300–308). Govinda Kaviraja came back with her and gave Narottama his guru's instruction:

“Be attentive in the service of the Sri Deity, honoring the Vaishnavas with body, mind and speech. Observe with care the holy days of Vishnu and the Vaishnavas; together with Ramachandra relish bhakti-rasa.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 11.277–278)

He also brought the “Gopala-virudavali” sent by Jiva; Narottama gave it to Ramachandra. When Jahnava asked for news of Gauda, Narottama could not say a word for tears, and Ramachandra answered that the Lord's dear ones had almost all gone into concealment (11.340–342). Narottama and Ramachandra accompanied Jahnava through Budhari, Ekachakra, Katwa and Yajigrama to Srikhanda; in Yajigrama Srinivasa put them in charge of all arrangements (11.361–750).

Then Srinivasa took Narottama and Ramachandra to Navadvipa. The Lord's old servant Ishana — it was he who had called Srinivasa through Narottama (12.127) — embraced them and the next day led them round the holy places, the nine islands of Navadvipa; Srinivasa took Narottama with him, “one with him in soul.” At parting Ishana made known by a sign that they would not meet again, and on the way to Srikhanda they heard that Ishana had left this world (13.11, 13.21).

Vira Hambira came to Srinivasa in Yajigrama. Seeing Narottama's radiance, he said to himself: “This prabhu is surely Thakura Mahashaya” (13.42) — and fell at his feet. At parting the king tearfully repented that, by stealing the books, he had once caused him pain, and Narottama replied:

“From that wicked deed came victory everywhere. Now keep all that in mind no longer; be diligent in acquiring the jewel of bhakti.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 13.131–132)

Afterwards Srinivasa came again to Kheturi with Narottama and Ramachandra; here a disputatious brahmana, seeing them in sankirtana, took shelter of Srinivasa in tears, and Srinivasa entrusted him to Narottama, “[his very] life” (13.165–168). Virachandra, Nityananda's son, also came to Kheturi on his way to Vraja: Thakura Mahashaya came out to meet him with great joy, Virachandra danced in the sankirtana in Gauranga's courtyard and, having said something to Narottama in private, left for Vraja (13.299–301); according to one of the biographies, he came “to increase Sri Narottama's joy,” and the festival went on for several days.

Ramachandra, Narottama and Govinda lived in Kheturi, and the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that all three “are always intoxicated with sankirtana” (14.30). Jiva wrote to them from Vrindavana a joint letter: “To those named Sri Ramachandra Kaviraja, Sri Narottama Dasa and Sri Govinda Dasa, praised by all the Vaishnavas…” (14.32). Narottama met Srinivasa in Budhari; together they attended the installation of Sri Radha-vinoda in Govinda Chakravarti's house in Borakuli, where Virachandra, “becoming still in the rapture of the dance, weeps, embracing Narottama” (14.137); and later, having visited Kheturi, Srinivasa said something in private “to Narottama, dearer to him than life” (14.159).

Brahmanas at the Thakura's Feet

After the festival Narottama's fame spread through the whole Vaishnava world. Eminent brahmanas became his disciples — Ramakrishna Acharya and Ganganarayana Chakravarti — and many learned devotees of the region; these two became the most important preachers among his disciples. The “Narottama-vilasa” (12) lists the branches and shoots of Narottama's tree, and the “Bhakti-ratnakara” speaks of them in songs: “Sri Narottama's disciple is Ramakrishna Acharya, a supreme pandita,” for whom “the two feet of Narottama are his all,” and “Sri Thakura Narottama is the purifier of the fallen; his disciple is Ganganarayana Chakravarti” (15.121–128).

Not everyone was pleased. A smarta pandita insulted Narottama before his own students, calling him a shudra — and his body began to rot with leprosy. In despair he went to drown himself in the Ganga, but that night Durga-devi came to him in a dream: “Fool, you took a mahabhagavata for a shudra… Go to his feet and ask his pardon.” The next morning, with a cloth round his neck as a sign of humility, he fell in tears at Narottama's feet. The Thakura's company gradually healed him; on Narottama's advice he began to serve Krishna and became deeply attached to him. The disease was not a “punishment of the Goddess” but the fruit of offending a Vaishnava; and Durga, Mahamaya, is the Lord's maidservant, and so she herself sends the offender to the feet of His devotee. The “Narottama-vilasa” (9) tells the same.

Once Narottama and Ramachandra Kaviraja were on their way to bathe in the Padmavati when they met two young brahmanas, Harirama and Ramakrishna, sons of Shivananda Acharya, a zamindar of the village of Goyasgaram. At their father's order they were leading goats and a buffalo to be sacrificed to the Goddess at the Durga-puja in their home. The radiance of the two Vaishnavas captivated the youths. Narottama explained to them the meaning of the “Bhagavata”: the rites of karma-kanda in the modes of passion and ignorance, with violence to animals, do not elevate — even one who reaches heaven falls from it, and one who kills animals destroys his own soul; and every soul is Krishna's energy. Give up such worship, he said, and serve the Supreme Lord without selfish motive. The brothers set the animals free, bathed in the Padma, came to the temple of Mahaprabhu, and the next morning, with shaven heads, received the mantra of Radha-Krishna: Harirama from Ramachandra Kaviraja, Ramakrishna from Narottama.15

Shivananda was enraged. Finding his sons in Narottama's ashrama at Kheturi — with tilaka, a tulasi-mala round the neck and a shikha — he summoned from Mithila the smarta pandita Murari. But by their guru's mercy the sons refuted all his arguments from scripture, showing that a Vaishnava stands above a brahmana, and the pandita fled. And that night the Goddess reproached Shivananda in a dream for his enmity towards Vaishnavas: “Sri Hari is the master of all… Go to Narottama and beg forgiveness.”

Ganganarayana Chakravarti, a famous learned brahmana of Gambhila, listened attentively to the Gosvamis' siddhanta from Narottama, took shelter at his feet, and then studied the Gosvamis' books deeply. Jagannatha Acharya, a worshipper of Durga, also came to him: Durga herself told him in a dream to go to Narottama, saying, “Krishna is my master and my guru.” He came to Kheturi and bowed down; Narottama smiled and said, “Great is your fortune — Krishna's mercy is upon you,” and initiated him into the mantra of Radha-Krishna. Jagannatha became one of his dearest and most trusted disciples; the “Prema-vilasa” (19) also tells of him.

The smartas complained to Raja Narasimha, the ruler of Pakkapalli: “Narottama is a shudra, yet he makes brahmanas his disciples. Let this continue, and we shall perish like the Yadus.” With the raja and the digvijayi pandita Rupa Narayana they set out for Kheturi.16 Ramachandra Kaviraja and Ganganarayana learned that they had stopped for the night in the bazaar at Kumarapura, and opened stalls there — a potter's and a pan-seller's. They addressed the smartas in pure Sanskrit and defeated them all in debate, Rupa Narayana included. Learning that these were Narottama's disciples, the raja said: “If even his ordinary disciples defeat you, there is no point in going to him himself.” That night Durga appeared to the raja and Rupa Narayana in a dream with a sword and told them to take shelter of Narottama. In the morning they came and found him in the temple of Gauranga, absorbed in chanting the name. Narottama received them respectfully and humbly: “I am insignificant, while you are famed for your learning, your wisdom and a king's riches. How fortunate I am that such learned and noble men have come to me; what service can I do for you?” They fell at his feet, begging forgiveness, and after a few days he initiated them into the mantra of Radha-Krishna. The “Prema-vilasa” (19) also tells of the raja's conversion; it also contains the tradition of a sacred thread that appeared in Narottama's heart.

How, then, could a kayastha be a guru to brahmanas? This is no violation and no “protest” against social order. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati explains in the “Anubhashya”:

“Sri Thakura Narottama, Shyamananda and other gurus who were true brahmanas were in fact pure brahmanas themselves. That is exactly why brahmanas by birth such as Sri Ganganarayana and Ramakrishna recognised them as pure ‘brahmanas’ fit to be gurus.” (“Anubhashya” on CC Madhya 24.325)

Mahabhagavatas, he says elsewhere, are nishkinchana paramahamsas beyond varnashrama who take shelter of Krishna alone — and at once he quotes Narottama's words from the “Prarthana”: “One who regards the associates of Gauranga as eternally perfect goes to the son of the king of Vraja” (“Anubhashya” on CC Madhya 11.67).

Nor was there any worldly entanglement in Narottama's accepting many disciples. Of those who think so, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes:

“Sri Rupa, Sri Sanatana, Sri Jiva, Sri Raghunatha Dasa and the Lord's other associates, the great souls, as well as Sriman Narottama, Srila Madhva, Ramanuja and others, accepted many disciples and gave instruction by writing books. Many foolish people imagine that all this is an obstacle to bhakti and a wave of worldly objects, and so they become offenders at the feet of genuine akinchana devotees.” (“Anubhashya” on CC Madhya 7.130)

An acharya's power is not measured by the number of his disciples: in one line there are both hermits who delight in solitary service (viviktanandi) and preachers who enlarge the community (goshthyanandi).

Kirtana and Songs

Narottama's ashrama, according to the late reference work “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” was at Bhajantuli, about two miles from the capital of Kheturi. He preached above all through kirtana. He introduced his own style into sankirtana — garanhati — and this style helped to spread bhakti through the land; Srinivasa had the manohara-shahi style and Shyamananda the reneti; today all three are lost. Srinivasa preached both through the “Bhagavata” and through kirtana, Narottama and Shyamananda mainly through kirtana. According to the “Narottama-vilasa” (6), Narottama created his style before the Deity of Gauranga, and gandharvas came to listen.

Narottama's songs are collected in the “Prarthana” and the “Prema-bhakti-chandrika”; one of the biographies also names a book of kirtanas, the “Nama-sankirtana.” A pranama to his guru Lokanatha is also his. These books have been reprinted countless times and have influenced all who walk the path of bhakti: in them is the life of the devotees and songs for every mood. His influence reached even distant Manipur: there it is acknowledged that Vaishnavism spread by his spiritual power, and his songs are heard in every household. The “Prema-vilasa” (17) tells of the “Prema-bhakti-chandrika.”17

The biographies quote much from his songs. In his songs he prays to Nityananda (“Ara kabe nitai chand…”) and to Advaita, remembers his guru (“Ha ha prabhu Lokanatha…”: only by your mercy will Narottama's longing for the service of Radha-Govinda and Chaitanya be fulfilled), laments bitterly that he did not serve the feet of the nine Gosvamis, among whom he names Bhugarbha and Lokanatha (“Hari hari, ki mora karama-gati manda…”), sings of Rupa and Sanatana and of Gauranga (“Bane te thake ha Gauranga…”; “Vrajendra-nandana yei, shachi-suta haila sei” — “He who is the son of the king of Vraja has become the son of Shachi”). The songs about Sri Rupa-manjari — “Sri rupa-manjari-pada sei mora sampada…,” “Shuniyachhi sadhu-mukhe…,” “Ei nava-dasi bali…,” “Sri-rupa-pashchate ami…” — speak of service in Rupa's footsteps. The “Prema-bhakti-chandrika” opens with a mangalacharana to Rupa, and from it too comes “Shuniya govinda-raba…”; the biographies also quote the lines “Jaya sanatana rupa prema-bhakti-rasa-kupa…” and “Ana katha ana vyatha….” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” quotes his lines on the devotee's only wealth:

“Thakura Narottama says: ‘My wealth is Nityananda’; ‘The feet of Sri Radha and Krishna are the wealth of my life’; ‘Glory to You, Purifier of the fallen! Give me this wealth: apart from You nothing is dear to me’; ‘The feet of Sri Rupa-manjari are my treasure, my service and worship, the wealth of my life.’” (“Anubhashya” on CC Adi 13.124)

And the “Bhakti-ratnakara” quotes his verse on the Lord's two shaktis:

“Through one shakti, headed by Sri Rupa, the Lord reveals these books; through another shakti, named Sri Srinivasa, He spreads them. When will He who mercifully manifested these two shaktis on earth — the ocean of mercy Sri Chaitanya — come before my eyes?” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.234)

In these songs is his soul. He calls himself a “chandala” and by other self-abasing names, just as Mahaprabhu called Himself “a Mayavadi sannyasi without prema”: devotees hide their greatness. Narottama is the best follower of Rupa Gosvami, “the first among the followers of Rupa,” the servant of Rupa, Raghunatha and Jiva, who accepted Rupa as his treasure of prema. In one of his songs he draws a ladder of mercy: without shelter at Jahnava's feet there is no mercy of Nityananda; without it the desires for enjoyment do not leave; while they remain there is no mercy of Rupa and Raghunatha, and without that no attachment to the youthful Couple of Vraja.

Srinivasa was Narottama's friend, his equal in spirit, and yet Narottama in a song asked him for the company of his disciple: “Prabhu Srinivasa Acharya, be merciful — Narottama Dasa begs for the company of Ramachandra.” This shows how he loved Srinivasa himself. In the “Prarthana” he prayed for Srinivasa's mercy also when detractors condemned the Acharya's second marriage. And Ramachandra Kaviraja was the closest companion of his preaching and bhajana, his second self; Narottama held him dearer than his own life, and Srinivasa, Narottama and Ramachandra were of one heart and mind. Initiating Ramachandra, Srinivasa said to him of Narottama: “He is one eye, you are the second eye; you both are my eyes, you two are my two arms” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 8.546) — and at the very name of Narottama prema awoke in Ramachandra. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says of Ramachandra:

“Ramachandra Kaviraja, full of all virtues, is the one with whom Narottama Mahashaya is one in soul.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.269)

Narahari also quotes a verse from Govinda Kaviraja's drama “Sangita-madhava,” where Ramachandra is called “truly one” with the renowned Narottama (1.270), and another about the two “who became a pair through great mutual love” (1.277). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that Thakura Narottama prayed for Ramachandra's company birth after birth, and that Ramachandra was the chief and dearest companion of Thakura Mahashaya and Srinivasa Acharya in preaching and in bhajana (on CC Adi 11.51). The “Prema-vilasa” (17) describes their friendship and the order of their bhajana. As once Rupa, Sanatana and Raghunatha, as Lokanatha and Bhugarbha, so Narottama and Ramachandra showed the bhajana of like-minded friends, without a trace of rivalry — though they did not necessarily live in one hut.

When Srinivasa came to Gauda, Narottama and Shyamananda were with him, and a flood of Hari-kirtana arose. Srinivasa, Narottama and the other acharyas spread sankirtana by the mercy and under the guidance of Jahnava, and also of Vishnupriya; Jahnava they accepted as jagad-guru and considered they had fulfilled the purpose of life by hearing Hari-katha from her.

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” pictures the Thakura's life in Kheturi: he served the Vaishnavas with body, mind and words, his festivals of sankirtana never ceased, and in that ocean of happiness all bathed, down to the lowliest; Gauranga's associates in Gauda rejoiced on seeing him, and Jahnava was pleased at the very name “Sri Thakura Mahashaya” and mercifully came to Kheturi herself (1.427–434). By the Lord's will he accepted many disciples, and whomever he favoured attained every perfection (1.435–437). Ramachandra's brother Govinda Kaviraja sang of him:

“Glory, glory, glory to Thakura Narottama, the great king of prema-bhakti, whose minister, one with him in body, is Ramachandra Kaviraja! Prema is the jewel of his crown, his ornaments the succession of bhavas, with which every limb of his shines; on the royal throne in Kheturi he sits, and with him the assembly of devotees.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 1.439–440)

And Narahari himself, in songs of the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” retells the Thakura's life — from his boyhood tears over Gora to the kirtana in which Advaita, Nityananda and Gaurachandra dance with Their associates — speaks of his oneness with Srinivasa: “One soul, only the bodies different” (14.218) — and prays: “Will there be such a day, [when] I shall be sold at Narottama's feet?” (14.226)

Separation and Withdrawal

Ramachandra, with the blessing of Narottama and Srinivasa — by one of the biographies, at their bidding — went again to Vrindavana and some months later entered the eternal pastimes; Srinivasa, unable to bear separation from his beloved disciple, also left this world. Narottama first learned of Ramachandra's departure, and soon after, of Srinivasa's. In great separation he composed the song “Ye anila prema-dhana karuna prachura…” — “He who brought the treasure of prema, boundlessly merciful…” — on his separation from Srinivasa; all the devotees sing it. The “Narottama-vilasa” (11) gives another of his laments as well — “Gaurangera sahachara…” — about the associates of Gauranga.

It was the same sorrow that lived in his songs all his life: he had come into the world when the Lord had already withdrawn. Vrindavana Dasa Thakura grieves that he did not see the pastimes of the Lord as a scholar:

“I am a fallen sinner — it was not my lot to be born at that time and see those divine pastimes.” (CB Madhya 1.399)

And Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on this verse quotes Narottama's “Prarthana”: “Not having obtained the company of those associates, Narottama Dasa weeps,” and: “When Gaura, Nityananda, Advaita and the devotees appeared in Nadia, I was not born.”

Soon his own hour came. Almost drowning in the ocean of separation, Narottama took leave of the Deities and went with Govinda and others to Budhari; he spent a day there in kirtana and then came to Gambhila on the Ganga. There he entered the temple of Mahaprabhu and told the devotees to sing kirtana. After the sankirtana, bowing to the Ganga in tears, he entered the water and, going in a little way, asked that all directions be filled with loud chanting of the holy name. Ramakrishna Acharya and Ganganarayana Chakravarti led two kirtanas in two places. He asked them to wash his body with Ganga water — and as they were about to do so, he, absorbed in the chanting of the name, withdrew from worldly eyes into the waters of the Ganga. The “Narottama-vilasa” says:

“From Budhari he went quickly to Gambhila, bathed in the Ganga and sat in the Ganga's water. He ordered Ramakrishna and Ganganarayana, ‘Both of you, wash my body.’ How could they wash him? As soon as they touched him, he dissolved like milk into the waters of the Ganga. Before everyone's eyes he quickly disappeared — this is utterly unfathomable: who could understand it?” (“Narottama-vilasa” 11.330–333)

The waves of the Ganga surged up, the gods showered flowers from heaven, and from all sides rose the cry, “Hari! Hari!” Narahari calls it Sri Mahashaya's hidden withdrawal. Thakura Mahashaya left this world as the Lord's eternal associates leave it — he withdrew.

Earlier, according to the same book, there had been another pastime. In Gambhila Narottama had a funeral pyre made ready, stayed silent for three days and, as Narahari says, “in the eyes of people, separated from his body” (11.232). The brahmana detractors were already rejoicing: here, they said, was the price of brahmana disciples. But Ganganarayana, taking pity on them, prayed at the pyre: “Prabhu, save them,” — and the Thakura at once returned to his body and, crying “Radha-Krishna! Chaitanya!”, rose from the pyre shining like the sun. The detractors repented and fell at Ganganarayana's feet, and Narottama gave them bhakti. The Lord's eternal associate is not subject to the laws of the body: he showed this pastime for people's eyes — for the sake of those very detractors.

The day of his departure is the krishna-panchami of the month of Kartika; according to our calendar (Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math), the krishna-panchami of the month of Damodara (≈ Kartika); in 2026 it fell on 30 October. The sources do not give the year of his departure.18 One of the biographies says that Vishvanatha Chakravarti was active some sixty years after Narottama's withdrawal.

After his departure his disciples held festivals in Gambhila and in Kheturi. In the kirtana at Kheturi everyone suddenly saw Narottama dancing; after dancing a little he slipped away unseen, and later, appearing in dreams, consoled those close to him (“Narottama-vilasa” 11.338–355).

Legacy

Narottama's disciplic line reached Srila Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura: Narottama — Ganganarayana Chakravarti — Krishnacharana Chakravarti — Radharamana Chakravarti — Vishvanatha; he is the fourth from Narottama. Vishvanatha named his line in an auspicious verse:

“Bowing to the feet of my gurus, full of great love — Rama, Krishna and Ganga — I praise Srila Narottama, Natha and Sri Gauranga Prabhu.”

“Rama” here is Radharamana, “Krishna” is Krishnacharana, “Ganga” is Ganganarayana, “Natha” is Lokanatha. Vishvanatha wrote his “Sankalpa-kalpadruma” “under the guidance of Sri Lokanatha and Sri Narottama” of his line, and among his minor works is the “Sri Narottamashtaka,” a hymn to Narottama in nine stanzas; Narahari too quotes two of its stanzas in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (11.16–17). And in the line of shiksha — the handing down of truth itself — as Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati gives it, Narottama, together with Srinivasa and Shyamananda, stands between Krishnadasa Kaviraja and Vishvanatha: Mahaprabhu — Svarupa Damodara — Rupa and Sanatana (with Raghunatha Dasa, Raghunatha Bhatta and Gopala Bhatta) — Jiva — Krishnadasa Kaviraja — Narottama — Vishvanatha.

With the departure of Srinivasa, Narottama, Shyamananda and Rasikananda, the third of its “dark ages” began for Bengal Vaishnavism: darkness descended on Gaudiya Vaishnavism, and apasampradayas multiplied.

But the Gaudiya Vaishnavas of later generations kept Narottama's songs as something intimate. Srila Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji considered the “Prarthana” and the “Prema-bhakti-chandrika” his everything and often sang Narottama's song “Keno va achhaye prana…”; Srila Vamshidasa Babaji quoted the “Prema-bhakti-chandrika” (“Shuniya govinda-raba…”). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati as a schoolboy read only the “Prarthana,” the “Prema-bhakti-chandrika” and his father's books. In Bogra he spoke of North Bengal, once blessed by Narottama. And on his last day in this world he asked Srila B. R. Sridhara Maharaja to sing “Sri rupa-manjari-pada,” a song he dearly loved, and said: “Narottama Dasa Thakura accepted the understanding of Rupa and Raghunatha — better to live by it.” The songs of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura are of the same essence as Narottama's; and Srila Akinchana Dasa Babaji said that Sridhara Maharaja's writings too are not different from Narottama's. Srila Krishnadasa Babaji himself gave no one initiation, yet, seeing the countless people blessed by Narottama, Bhaktivinoda and other great souls, he never presumed to say that their company did those people no good: he understood that this was their calling.

He is remembered also by Narahari Chakravarti, the author of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” and the “Narottama-vilasa.” Near the end of the “Namamrita-samudra,” his prayers to the Lord's associates, he calls on him together with Srinivasa and Shyamananda:

“O Srinivasa! Narottama! Shyamananda! Be merciful to me together with your followers — I am very wicked.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 270)

Champaka-manjari

In Krishna's eternal pastimes Narottama is Champaka-manjari, who always assists Sri Rupa-manjari in the service of Radha and Krishna; out of mercy for conditioned souls she came into this world. According to the “Prema-vilasa” (11), Sri Radha Herself bestowed on him this service and this name.19

So Thakura Mahashaya, called by the Lord before his birth, received prema from the hands of the Padmavati, served his guru as a servant of servants, brought the Gosvamis' books to Gauda, revealed in Kheturi six Deities and in his kirtana Mahaprabhu Himself with His associates, and in his songs left to the Gaudiya Vaishnavas the path of the followers of Rupa. He is called one of the three acharyas who preserved the Gosvamis' heritage — and the Gaudiya Vaishnavas sing his songs as something intimate to this day.
